strengths: The paper proposes an interesting critic-side use of action sequences: a causal Transformer predicts returns for multiple action-prefix lengths while retaining a reactive, step-based SAC policy.
The empirical scope includes all 50 Meta-World ML1 tasks plus dense and sparse box-pushing, and the reported aggregate Meta-World and dense box-pushing results are strong.
Per-task learning curves, several policy-component ablations, an MLP-critic control, and detailed hyperparameter tables provide useful diagnostic information.
weaknesses: The central variance-reduction justification is not established. The analysis assumes approximately i.i.d. rewards, ignores discounting and temporal correlations, and only changes the asymptotic variance from O(N) to O(N/3), not its order. More importantly, averaging gradients from different prediction heads and targets does not generally inherit the variance formula for averaging scalar returns because the gradients have different, correlated Jacobians.

The mathematical specification is internally inconsistent. Equation (6) appears to compare every prefix prediction with G^(n), although the surrounding text says prefixes use G^(1),...,G^(n). Equation (3) and Appendix B also use inconsistent summation limits. These ambiguities affect the core algorithm rather than merely presentation.

The mechanism connecting multi-step auxiliary predictions to policy improvement is insufficiently analyzed. With causal masking, the first-token Q(s,a) used by the actor cannot attend to future actions and is directly supervised by the one-step target; longer-prefix losses influence it only through shared parameters. The paper provides neither theory nor representation/gradient analysis showing why this yields the claimed benefit.

The experiments do not isolate the main claimed ingredients. There is no systematic ablation of return horizon, one-step versus multi-step training, gradient-level versus target-level averaging, causal Transformer versus a recurrent or parameter-matched sequence critic, or the critic with and without action sequences. The reported ablations also use inconsistent subsets of tasks.

Evaluation rigor is inadequate for the strength of the claims. The manuscript does not clearly state seed counts for the main experiments, define uncertainty bands, report confidence intervals or statistical tests for aggregate scores, or explain the unusual IQM procedure described as requiring 75% convergence.

Comparison fairness is difficult to assess because algorithms use substantially different architectures, normalization, update schedules, batch sizes, learning starts, and other hyperparameters. T-SAC also introduces policy-network changes in addition to the critic, while compute cost, parameter counts, wall-clock time, and tuning budgets are not reported.

Some conclusions contradict or exceed the evidence. T-SAC is called state of the art on sparse box-pushing despite gSDE scoring 60% versus T-SAC's 58% in Table 1. Claims of sample efficiency and efficient training are weak given training budgets up to 20 million interactions and the absence of compute comparisons.

Reproducibility remains limited: the algorithm pseudocode omits important details such as twin-critic aggregation, the precise soft-value target, entropy treatment in sequence returns, terminal handling, padding/masking, sampling of sequence lengths, and update scheduling. No code or artifact is identified.

The contribution is fairly close to the cited TOP-ERL Transformer critic and established multi-step auxiliary learning; the paper does not sharply distinguish the technical novelty beyond pairing a related critic with a step-based SAC actor. Overall, the promising empirical signal is not yet supported by sufficiently sound analysis or controlled evaluation for a top-tier acceptance.

strengths: The paper explores an interesting direction: using a Transformer critic to learn from action-sequence prefixes and multiple return horizons while retaining a reactive SAC policy.
The empirical scope includes all 50 Meta-World tasks plus dense and sparse box-pushing environments, and the reported aggregate success rates are promising.
The appendix provides per-task learning curves and extensive hyperparameter tables, while the ablations attempt to separate the effects of the Transformer critic and policy modifications.
The manuscript is generally readable, and the architecture diagrams make the intended policy and critic structures relatively accessible.
weaknesses: The central variance-reduction justification is not technically established. The derivation analyzes an average of correlated multi-step targets under unrealistic i.i.d.-reward assumptions, whereas the implemented method averages gradients of losses attached to different sequence-prefix outputs. These are not generally equivalent estimators, so the analysis does not support the claimed benefit. Averaging gradients also does not clearly avoid the stated sparse-reward dilution problem.

The method specification is internally inconsistent. Equation 6 appears to compare every prefix prediction with the same n-step target, while the subsequent text says that distinct targets G(1),...,G(n) are used. The description also does not clearly specify twin critics, entropy in the bootstrap value, terminal handling, padding, or exactly which Transformer output trains the actor.

It is unclear how future action tokens improve the value used by the reactive actor. Under the stated causal Transformer, the first-token Q(s_t,a_t), which appears in the SAC policy objective, cannot attend to later actions. Longer-prefix outputs may therefore train auxiliary predictions without directly providing the claimed temporal reasoning to the actor; this crucial mechanism is neither explained nor tested.

The paper dismisses the need for importance sampling without adequately discussing the off-policy bias created by multi-step replay trajectories. Treating future behavior actions as explicit conditioning may define sequence-action values, but the connection between those values, the one-action policy objective, and the desired SAC value function requires a rigorous argument.

The evaluation does not convincingly establish state of the art. Comparisons omit several strong modern continuous-control and multi-step baselines, no direct comparison with standard n-step SAC is provided, and there is no comparison against parameter- or compute-matched Transformer/MLP critics.

The main contribution lacks essential ablations: return horizon, one-step versus multi-step training, target averaging versus gradient averaging, causal sequence direction, trajectory replay, critic capacity, and combinations of the proposed components. The presented SAC variants do not isolate these questions sufficiently.

Experimental reporting is inadequate for strong empirical claims. The number of seeds is mostly unspecified, Table 1 provides no uncertainty or significance estimates, box-pushing learning curves are absent, and the construction of the aggregate IQM results is insufficiently documented.

Baseline fairness is questionable because algorithms use substantially different training schedules, update counts, buffer configurations, normalization, discount factors, and entropy settings. In particular, box-pushing T-SAC uses no entropy term and thus is not actually the described soft actor-critic method, while its discount also differs from most baselines. Wall-clock cost, parameter counts, and total gradient updates are not reported.

Claims about sample efficiency, generalization, smooth value surfaces, robustness, and state-of-the-art performance are stronger than the evidence. Meta-World results extend to roughly 20 million interactions, the experiments do not directly test generalization or value-surface smoothness, and no perturbation-based robustness evaluation is given.

Reproducibility remains limited despite the hyperparameter tables: there is no code or complete pseudocode, and important implementation details of sequence construction, target computation, replay sampling, evaluation, and model architecture are missing. Several citation and presentation errors further reduce confidence in the paper's technical care.

strengths: The paper proposes an interesting critic-side use of action prefixes: a causal Transformer predicts returns at multiple horizons while the deployed policy remains reactive.
The empirical scope is notable, covering all 50 Meta-World ML1 tasks plus dense and sparse box-pushing, with especially promising results on several sparse or multi-phase tasks.
Per-task learning curves, implementation descriptions, hyperparameter tables, and several policy/critic ablations provide more evidence than a single aggregate benchmark result.
The method is practically motivated and the architecture is presented clearly enough to communicate its high-level operation.
weaknesses: The central variance-reduction justification is not established. Averaging gradients from losses with different targets is simply optimizing an averaged multi-task loss; it is not equivalent to averaging return estimators, and the return-variance derivation in Appendix B does not demonstrate reduced variance of these gradients or learned Q-values.

The off-policy correctness of the multi-step targets is unresolved. Targets use future actions stored under behavior policies without importance weighting or another correction, yet avoiding importance sampling is a central claim. No bias analysis or controlled experiment supports this choice.

Important equations are ambiguous or inconsistent. Equation 6 appears to use the same n-step target G^(n) for outputs associated with prefixes of lengths 1 through n, despite the surrounding text claiming distinct G^(1),...,G^(n) targets. The value target V, terminal handling, twin-critic construction, entropy term in bootstrapping, and exact policy-update pathway are also insufficiently specified.

The evaluation does not cleanly isolate the claimed contribution. There is no full factorial comparison separating Transformer architecture, action-prefix conditioning, and multi-step auxiliary targets, nor an ablation over return horizon. Comparisons to the closely related TOP-ERL and movement-primitive methods discussed in the paper are absent.

Baseline fairness is difficult to assess because algorithms use substantially different architectures, normalization, replay sizes, learning starts, update schedules, entropy settings, and even discount factors. T-SAC performs 100 critic epochs in settings where several baselines use one, but compute or update-matched comparisons are not reported.

Statistical reporting is incomplete: Table 1 gives point estimates without uncertainty or explicit seed counts, the construction of the aggregate percentages is unclear, and there are no confidence intervals or significance tests for the headline gains. Box-pushing evidence is particularly limited.

Claims of state-of-the-art performance, generalization, a smooth globally coherent value surface, and improved sample efficiency are stronger than the presented evidence; smoothness and value-estimation accuracy are not directly measured, and training extends to roughly 20 million interactions on Meta-World.

Reproducibility remains limited despite the hyperparameter tables: the algorithm pseudocode is too high-level to resolve the target-definition ambiguities, and no code or complete implementation details are provided. Overall, the promising empirical signal does not overcome the unresolved technical and evaluation issues required for a top-tier acceptance.

strengths: The paper proposes a practically interesting step-based actor–critic that combines a causal Transformer critic, action-prefix conditioning, and multi-horizon N-step supervision while retaining one-step policy execution.
The empirical scope is substantial: 50 Meta-World tasks, five MuJoCo tasks, and dense/sparse Box-Pushing, generally with multiple seeds and bootstrap confidence intervals.
Results on Meta-World and dense Box-Pushing are promising, with particularly strong performance on several difficult multi-phase tasks and favorable sample efficiency.

The paper includes useful ablations over horizon length, Transformer components, recurrent alternatives, action chunking, and target-update schedules, along with extensive hyperparameter and environment documentation in the reviewed manuscript :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/review_sample501_han_medium_20260920T175328Z/scratch/9b64b89895e344b998bca22f8f4caa40/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}.
The causal masking and explicit conditioning on realized replay actions provide a plausible way to train action-prefix value predictions without importance sampling.
weaknesses: The main empirical comparison is not sufficiently controlled. Most Meta-World baseline results are imported from prior publications or released runs, with different seed counts, training budgets, architectures, normalization choices, and potentially evaluation details, whereas T-SAC receives a targeted hyperparameter search. This weakens the state-of-the-art and sample-efficiency claims.

The critical missing ablation is a capacity-matched non-Transformer critic trained with exactly the same multi-horizon, prefix-conditioned objective and sampling scheme. The presented MLP comparison primarily concerns policy-side action chunking, while removing self-attention reportedly causes divergence. Consequently, the experiments do not cleanly establish whether gains arise from self-attention, multi-step auxiliary supervision, extra computation, or replay-window sampling.

The variance analysis does not justify the implemented optimization as strongly as claimed. Gradients from different horizons correspond to different outputs, targets, and losses, so they are not generally interchangeable unbiased estimators of one common gradient. Averaging them trivially reduces variance under the assumed equicorrelation model but can change the expected gradient and optimization objective. The claimed compounded benefit additionally invokes target-level averaging, which the method explicitly does not use.

The description repeatedly frames the critic as using trajectory context or historical control signals, but its input is an initial state followed by future realized actions, without intermediate states. This distinction matters, especially in stochastic or partially observable environments, and the evaluation is confined to largely deterministic simulators.

Important implementation details remain ambiguous despite the long appendix: the method is written using a single critic even though clipped double-Q estimation is central to SAC; the computation of the bootstrap expectation is not specified precisely; and Algorithm 1 does not clearly reconcile the claimed cached hard-target schedule with its per-update target refresh and soft-update pseudocode.

The target-free contribution is narrow and inconclusive: it is used only for locomotion, performs poorly on several tasks, becomes unstable in sparse Box-Pushing, and does not consistently outperform CrossQ or Polyak averaging. It should not be presented as a generally validated replacement for target networks.

Sparse Box-Pushing uses only four seeds and exhibits considerable instability, while T-SAC remains below TOP-ERL. More broadly, ablations are concentrated on one dense-reward task, leaving uncertainty about which components explain the Meta-World gains.

Code and trained models are promised only after acceptance. Given the method’s many task-specific settings, extensive tuning, unusual replay segmentation, masking, and target schedules, the current submission is difficult to independently reproduce or audit.

strengths: The core idea—training a causal Transformer critic on realized action prefixes with multi-horizon auxiliary targets—is intuitive and potentially useful for long-horizon control.

The empirical scope is broad, covering 50 Meta-World tasks, five MuJoCo tasks, and dense/sparse Box-Pushing; the manuscript also reports confidence intervals, per-task curves, several architectural ablations, and extensive hyperparameter tables.
The reported gains on Meta-World and dense Box-Pushing are substantial, and the paper candidly reports weaker MuJoCo performance and instability under sparse rewards.
weaknesses: The claimed methodological novelty is limited. “Gradient-level averaging” is simply the gradient of the mean of the per-horizon losses. Moreover, because causal masking prevents the first output Q(s_t,a_t)—the only output used by the actor—from seeing later actions, it still receives an ordinary one-step target; longer-horizon supervision affects policy learning only indirectly through parameter sharing.

The technical justification is substantially stronger than the evidence. Avoiding importance sampling is achieved by redefining higher-position outputs as values conditioned on realized replay actions, rather than solving conventional off-policy N-step evaluation. The paper does not establish that these auxiliary prefix values improve the actor-relevant Q(s,a), nor does it compare against standard off-policy multi-step corrections such as Retrace or TD(lambda).

The variance analysis relies on restrictive exchangeability, homoscedasticity, positive-correlation, and independence assumptions that are neither measured nor validated. Large portions analyze target-level averaging even though the method explicitly does not use averaged N-step targets. Some extensions to general covariance structures and the claimed compounded variance reduction are asserted with only sketches.

The experimental comparisons do not support the SOTA claims cleanly. Most Meta-World baselines are imported from prior publications or released runs, with different implementations, seed counts, preprocessing, hyperparameters, and interaction budgets. T-SAC receives a targeted grid search, while most baselines do not; CrossQ is capped at 10M steps on Box-Pushing while T-SAC runs for 20M.

Important controlled baselines are missing: a parameter- and compute-matched MLP trained with exactly the same realized-prefix multi-horizon objective, a Transformer with only one-step supervision, and established corrected multi-step SAC variants. The existing ablations are concentrated on one dense Box-Pushing task, often with only four seeds, and therefore do not isolate which design change explains the headline Meta-World gains.

The method simultaneously changes critic architecture, target definition, entropy treatment, policy normalization, policy delay, replay sampling, and update schedule. In particular, the critic estimates a non-soft return while the actor uses an entropy-regularized objective, but this deviation from SAC is not theoretically or empirically isolated.

Reproducibility is presently limited because code is promised only after acceptance. The update-to-data accounting is difficult to reconcile with tables listing 20 policy epochs, 100 critic epochs, and hundreds of collected transitions while the text claims UTD at most 1; the exact mapping among epochs, updates, windows, and token-level losses is unclear.

Several claims are overstated or unsupported: ML1 is described as testing task generalization although the reported setup appears to train separate single-task agents; smoother value estimates and more coherent control are claimed without direct measurements; and strong conclusions are drawn despite poor results on several MuJoCo tasks and only 58% success on sparse Box-Pushing. Overall, the reviewed manuscript :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/review_sample501_han_medium_20260920T175328Z/scratch/8225398e2621404fb96028054a2cbb4c/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"} contains promising empirical observations, but the novelty, technical support, comparison fairness, and reproducibility are insufficient for a top-tier acceptance.

strengths: Clear, practically interesting contribution: T-SAC combines a one-step SAC actor with a causal Transformer critic trained on realized action prefixes and multi-horizon returns.
Broad evaluation across 50 Meta-World tasks, five MuJoCo tasks, and dense/sparse Box-Pushing, generally using multiple seeds and bootstrap confidence intervals.
Strong results on difficult multi-phase Meta-World tasks and 96.8% success on dense Box-Pushing, with low update-to-data ratios and favorable sample efficiency relative to several episodic baselines.

Useful ablations cover causal masking, attention, supervision horizon, target-window sampling, recurrent alternatives, and policy-side action chunking; runtime and extensive hyperparameters are also reported.
The paper is candid about mixed locomotion performance, sparse-reward instability, and results below TOP-ERL on sparse Box-Pushing.
weaknesses: The variance analysis is overstated. Gradients from different horizons optimize different outputs and targets, so averaging them is not automatically an unbiased variance-reduced estimate of a common gradient. Key positive-correlation assumptions are asserted rather than empirically validated, while part of the target-averaging theory does not describe the implemented method.

The mechanism behind the actor improvement is insufficiently isolated. The actor uses only Q(s,a), whose causally masked first output cannot access later actions; benefits therefore arise indirectly through parameter sharing and auxiliary horizon losses. Matched auxiliary-loss MLP controls and value-error or credit-assignment diagnostics are missing.

Meta-World comparisons are not fully controlled: many baseline curves come from prior publications or official runs, seed counts and budgets differ, and the paper does not conclusively establish identical final-timestep success and aggregation protocols for all imported results. Describing ML1 averaging as task generalization is also questionable when separate task-specific agents appear to be trained.

Most diagnostic ablations use only dense Box-Pushing with four seeds. Sparse Box-Pushing is volatile, uses four seeds, and trails TOP-ERL; MuJoCo performance is mixed, including weak Hopper and Walker2d results.

Reproducibility is incomplete because code and models are only promised after acceptance. Important details remain unclear, including twin-critic/minimum-Q handling, bootstrap expectation estimation, precise termination masking, and the correspondence between the freeze-and-cache schedule and the pseudocode.
